blocks.text: Tool selection prompting covers how an agent chooses the right tool from among several available options for a given step, a decision that depends heavily on how clearly each tool is described and how well the prompt frames the actual decision the model needs to make.

This topic covers describing tools so a model can choose correctly, deciding among several plausible options, avoiding unnecessary tool use, handling the case where no available tool genuinely fits, and how tool naming and description quality directly affect selection accuracy.
1. What Tool Selection Prompting Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473540224-11333326.png

Tool selection is the decision an agent makes at each step of a plan, which of its available tools, if any, is the right one to use for this specific step, this decision quality depends heavily on how the tools are described within the prompt.
2. Describing Tools So the Model Can Choose Correctly

blocks.alt: Describing Tools So the Model Can Choose Correctly
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473540224-642117485.png

A tool description needs to communicate clearly what the tool actually does and when it should be used, a vague description, "utility tool," gives the model little basis for a correct choice, "search_web: searches the public internet for current information" gives it a clear, actionable basis for deciding.

code.content:
tools = [
    {"name": "search_web", "description": "Searches the public internet for current information"},
    {"name": "calculator", "description": "Performs precise numeric calculations"},
    {"name": "query_database", "description": "Queries the internal customer records database"},
]

blocks.text: 3. Choosing Among Several Plausible Options
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473540224-683111672.png

When several tools could plausibly apply to a given step, the prompt needs to give the model enough context about the actual task to distinguish between them, a question about a current event points toward search, a precise numeric computation points toward a calculator, a question about a specific customer record points toward the database tool.

blocks.text: 4. Avoiding Unnecessary Tool Calls
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473540224-673306781.png

Not every step genuinely needs a tool, a question the model can answer directly from its own knowledge does not need to trigger a search or database call, instructing the model to only use a tool when the task genuinely requires it avoids unnecessary latency and cost from reflexive, unneeded tool calls.
5. Handling the Case Where No Tool Fits

blocks.alt: Handling the Case Where No Tool Fits
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473540224-153960365.png

Sometimes none of the available tools genuinely address what a step actually requires, a well designed tool selection prompt includes explicit instructions for this case, state clearly that no available tool fits, rather than the model forcing an ill fitting tool choice just to produce some action.
6. Tool Naming and Description Quality Directly Affects Accuracy

blocks.alt: Tool Naming and Description Quality Directly Affects Accuracy
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473805494-567354429.png

This connects directly to the specificity principle covered throughout this course, two tools with similarly vague names and descriptions are much harder for a model to distinguish between correctly than two tools with clearly differentiated, specific descriptions, this concern is covered in much greater technical depth in the later Function Calling and Tool Calling module.

blocks.title: Tool description quality is often the actual root cause of selection errors
blocks.content: A model choosing the wrong tool is frequently not a reasoning failure at all, it is a direct consequence of ambiguous or overlapping tool descriptions that genuinely do not give the model enough basis to distinguish between them.

blocks.text: 7. A Worked Tool Selection Example

Given the task "what is the current stock price of a specific company," a well described search tool and calculator tool make the correct choice, search, straightforward, a poorly described pair of tools, both vaguely labeled as "data tools," would leave this same choice genuinely ambiguous.
8. Testing Tool Selection Accuracy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473805496-296452575.png

This connects to the metric-driven iteration process covered in an earlier module, running a set of realistic tasks against an agent tool set and measuring how often it selects the actually correct tool provides a concrete, measurable signal for whether tool descriptions need improvement.
9. Tool Selection vs Tool Execution

Tool selection is specifically the decision of which tool to use, tool execution, covered in a later topic in this module, covers the mechanics of actually calling that selected tool correctly with the right parameters, these are related but distinct steps in an agent overall action pipeline.
Worked Example

A team building a customer support agent gives it both a "lookup_account" tool and a "search_knowledge_base" tool with nearly identical vague descriptions, testing reveals the agent frequently picks the wrong one, querying account records for a general policy question and searching the knowledge base for a specific account lookup.

Rewriting both tool descriptions to be clearly distinct, "lookup_account: retrieves details for one specific customer account by ID" versus "search_knowledge_base: searches general product and policy documentation," resolves the confusion, tool selection accuracy on the same test set improves substantially once the descriptions actually give the model enough basis to distinguish between them.
Common Mistakes

items: Writing vague, overlapping tool descriptions that give the model little basis for choosing correctly between them
Triggering a tool call for a task the model could have answered directly from its own knowledge
Not providing an explicit fallback for the case where no available tool genuinely fits the actual need
Never measuring actual tool selection accuracy against a realistic set of test tasks

blocks.text: Practice

Write descriptions for three plausible but distinct tools, then write five realistic tasks and check by hand whether each tool description gives clear enough basis to determine the genuinely correct choice for each task, identifying any description that is too vague or overlapping.
Key Takeaway

Tool selection prompting depends heavily on clear, specific, well differentiated tool descriptions, avoiding unnecessary tool calls for tasks answerable directly, and explicit fallback instructions for when no available tool genuinely fits, with actual selection accuracy measured against realistic test cases rather than assumed.
